items.title: Now generally available: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs
items.summary:
Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning.

Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. 

Beyond one workload, one nodepool 

Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency. 

Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams:

  • Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted.

  • Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment.

  • Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable.

  • Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes. 

  • Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling.

Dynamic slicing architecture

GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube.

Dynamic super-slicing

GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency.

Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice.

Dynamic sub-slicing

Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy.

When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool.

Customer use cases

You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments.  

Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE 

GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation.

Getting started

Pre-provision nodepools

To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand. 

Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover.

This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes.

Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing 

After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations.

Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples.

Repair

When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies:

  • Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes.

  • Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions.

Next steps 

Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for  TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For  working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation.

items.title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
items.story_key: story|title:your experts have partners there s hope for keeping them together
items.content_excerpt: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used. Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove. Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates. Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method. In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers . Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. items.title: AWS Launches TorchNeuron to Run PyTorch Models on AWS Trainium Without Modifications
items.summary:
At the recent PyTorch Conference North America 2026, Amazon introduced TorchNeuron, a native PyTorch backend that enables developers to run existing PyTorch code on AWS Trainium AI chips with virtually no code modifications.

By Sergio De Simone

items.title: Benchmarking Speaker Embedders in the Sub-Second Regime for Real-Time Voice AI Agents
items.summary: Real-time Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression. Background sources include television audio, family members, and colleagues. Production denoisers remove non-stationary environmental noise effectively. Background speech shares the spectral characteristics of the target and passes through, causing false acceptances in downstream speaker verification (SV) and automatic speech recognition (ASR). We benchmark open-source speaker embedders TitaNet-Large, TitaNet-Small, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++, and SpeakerNet under a strict sub-second latency budget. Evaluation combines a controlled benchmark with a weighted human-annotated production set. Our controlled benchmark is built from real calls in which a second real speaker is injected into silence intervals at modulated amplitude. We report three findings. First, denoising before embedding is generally harmful and raises equal error rate (EER) across architectures. Second, truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment degrades every model. Third, roughly half of the TitaNet embedding is redundant for this task. Trailing dimensions encode population attributes such as language and gender. Such attributes carry little discriminative value in a demographically homogeneous user base. We distill these results into deployment guidance. Verification should run on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks. Thresholds should favor precision over F1. Truncated embeddings reduce the cost of similarity search.

items.title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
items.summary: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.

As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing and communication to maintain performance. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source, distributed inference-serving framework built to deploy models in multi-node environments at data center scale. It handles this routing and communication to maximize inference performance. Optimized for NVIDIA B200 GPUs, these recipes take the guesswork out of deployment, delivering up to 2x performance out of the box. They help developers bring Korea’s open models into production faster and turn them into broadly accessible AI for All services.

items.title: Migrating vLLM to the LibTorch Stable ABI
items.summary: How vLLM migrated its CUDA build and compiled dependencies to the LibTorch Stable ABI, enabling compatible PyTorch upgrades without rebuilding vLLM.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:migrating vllm to the libtorch stable abi
items.content_excerpt: vLLM relies heavily on PyTorch, with frequent calls to LibTorch in its C++ backend. As a result, changes to LibTorch’s binary interface may require vLLM to be rebuilt and relinked, even when the APIs remain unchanged. What if we could update LibTorch without rebuilding vLLM? That’s where the LibTorch Stable ABI comes in. With a LibTorch Stable ABI, updating LibTorch does not require rebuilding or updating vLLM in order to keep using it. Instead, we could swap out the torch wheel and import it directly into our vLLM package. As of v0.33.0, vLLM publishes LibTorch ABI Stable CUDA wheels. Left: Unstable ABI—new torch requires vLLM to rebuild. Right: Stable ABI—vLLM can import new torch directly. Note: Compatibility between vLLM and PyTorch still depends on other factors, including Python APIs, GPU-related requirements (such as the minimum supported CUDA version), and third-party dependencies. The LibTorch Stable ABI addresses binary compatibility but does not eliminate these other constraints. An application binary interface (ABI) defines how compiled code interacts with a library: how functions are called, data is laid out, and symbols are named. Even if an API looks the same in source code, an ABI change can force extensions to rebuild. A stable ABI preserves a supported set of binary interfaces across compatible versions, so extensions that use them can keep working without a rebuild. PyTorch's LibTorch Stable ABI has three layers: a stable C shim exposing selected LibTorch APIs, C++ wrappers that make the shim easier to use, and headeronly utilities in torch::headeronly that do not link against libtorch.so . Before the Stable ABI, a new PyTorch release could require a vLLM rebuild, delaying support for the new version and its features. With the Stable ABI, the same vLLM wheel can work across compatible PyTorch releases, letting users upgrade sooner and reducing rebuilds for package distributors. For developers, this means you can update and rebuild PyTorch, then test those changes in vLLM without rebuilding vLLM. Left: vLLM needs to change as LibTorch changes. Right: vLLM can change independent of LibTorch. The LibTorch Stable ABI is a limited subset of all of LibTorch. While many common ops are already supported through the C shim and through the higher level C++ convenience wrappers, not all are. For example, is_pinned() lacked a stable equivalent during the migration. Thankfully, there is a general-purpose torch_call_dispatcher C shim that allows us to

items.title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
items.story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. items.title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

items.title: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL
items.summary: Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.318
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session
  • Added assume_role on mantle upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
  • Added an effort option to a mod's $.model.fork, so a quick side job can run at low whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent
  • Added the date a stored claude.ai sign-in ends to claude auth status (loginExpiresAt) and to claude -p JSON results (credential_expires_at)
  • Added a one-line stderr warning to claude -p text output, starting 10 days before a stored claude.ai sign-in ends
  • Fixed --continue sometimes losing the earlier conversation after a malformed tool call's retries ran out (regression in 2.1.314)
  • Fixed macOS sessions with many running Bash commands stalling while memory grew
  • Fixed permission prompts being answered by keys typed just after sending a message, or before a slow prompt appeared
  • Fixed /logout, claude auth logout and claude mcp remove reporting success, and changes to trust, consent or MCP settings being dropped with no word, when the config file could not be updated on a shared network home directory
  • Fixed jobs exiting with Not logged in when another terminal or host signs in again to the same account and organization on the same home
  • Fixed claude mcp add and remove writing the config without its lock: they now wait for it or exit 1, though another job's save can still replace a saved server
  • Fixed claude plugin commands exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed claude plugin validate passing a custom-named marketplace file that claude plugin marketplace add rejects
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers that exit on the version probe being re-probed on every start; a server that dies in under 3s for its own reason is also pinned to the legacy handshake for 7 days
  • Fixed sessions being refused at startup by an allowedProviders list that another login on the same machine had stored
  • Fixed idle compaction replacing a conversation with a reply that was not a summary
  • Fixed the "Now using usage credits" notice reappearing about every 30 seconds while a background subagent is running
  • Fixed custom slash commands that fail, or that only Claude can invoke, printing nothing in claude -p and SDK sessions
  • Fixed claude -p and Agent SDK sessions reporting success when an API error cut off a reply while a mod hooked turn.step
  • Fixed a message sent right after a model change still running after Stop in headless sessions: Stop now cancels or stops it as it would a queued message
  • Fixed a deleted session transcript being re-created with its last prompt when an idle non-interactive session exited
  • Fixed claude remote-control hosts, the background daemon and self-hosted runners failing to start new sessions (spawn ENOENT) after an update or version cleanup removed the binary of a still-running process
  • Fixed a running Claude Code process owned by another user (for example one left by sudo claude) being treated as dead by version cleanup, which could delete its binary
  • Fixed /remote-control showing a session as available after a failed connection
  • Fixed /design revoke reporting success when the request failed with a 404
  • Fixed a shell command approved after a self-hosted runner or cloud session restart running in the session's start folder, not the folder it was asked in; if that folder can't be entered, it is not run
  • Fixed Claude not being told when an approved connector tool was unavailable after a cloud session restart
  • Fixed cloud sessions being stopped in the middle of a turn when the service refuses uploads for several minutes
  • Fixed variables a Setup hook writes to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE not reaching the Bash tool in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed the iPhone app showing a cloud session's turn as finished while it kept running, after a response was cut off at a tool call or a refused image or document was removed
  • Fixed a restarted session re-sending a message that failed with an API error, ahead of the newer message waiting behind it
  • Fixed a restarted session dropping its interrupted turn when the restart came right after Claude read a large image or retried a tool call
  • Fixed every connection failing when the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file is empty, not PEM, or starts with a damaged certificate: readable certificates are now used, with a warning on stderr
  • Fixed workflows re-running finished agents when resumed after a usage limit
  • Fixed /mcp in cloud sessions counting tools the model can't use; a server's row now shows how many of its tools are available
  • Fixed a duplicate notification when Claude left the status field out of a PushNotification call
  • Fixed the error for a too-large image in a request with more than 20 images always saying the limit was 2000px; it now shows the API's limit
  • Fixed the runtime in background shell details not updating while the dialog is open
  • Fixed a mod's turn.step hook making a stopped reply finish as a success in headless runs
  • Fixed retention cleanup leaving a home that only runs claude -p with no ~/.claude.json backup: it now takes a fresh backup before deleting the last good one
  • Fixed the stored login being replaced by an empty file when a network home directory has no room left for data but still takes new files
  • Fixed tokens from setup-token being refused at start on machines with forceLoginOrgUUID, when the token belongs to a permitted organization
  • Fixed non-interactive launches replacing a ~/.claude.json that isn't valid JSON with defaults; the start now fails, says how to restore the file, and leaves it as is (#87551)
  • Fixed an empty ~/.claude.json with no backup being reported as corrupted; Claude Code now starts as it does when the file is missing
  • Fixed the restore command printed for a damaged or missing ~/.claude.json naming an empty or cut-off backup, or failing on a read-only file
  • Fixed the sign-in failure when a stored claude.ai login reaches its time limit: it now says so, and in claude -p names claude auth login and claude setup-token
  • Improved how ~/.claude.json, settings files and the stored login survive saves on shared network home directories: they are less often deleted, briefly emptied or replaced by a near-empty or older copy
  • Improved sessions on network file systems to look again when the configuration file is wrongly reported as missing, so fewer start without your MCP servers and trusted folders
  • Improved MCP tool errors: a call made before the tool is loaded now returns its input schema
  • Improved the reliability of git commits and pull request creation when the Bash tool runs macOS's built-in /bin/bash
  • Improved "Ask your admin for more usage" in the usage limit menu to send the request in one step
  • Improved how fast remote sessions reconnect after a pause or sleep
  • Improved You should know toasts to say "try again" instead of "press 2", which only works in the terminal
  • Improved auto-update reliability: a brief network failure while verifying a release is now retried right away instead of waiting for the next check
  • Improved unattended runs (claude -p, SDK apps) to stop rewriting ~/.claude.json on every run when nothing in it changed
  • Changed Claude Code to no longer install or update the IDE extension when started in an IDE terminal; use /ide from an outside terminal or your editor's extensions view
  • Changed subagents to stop instead of switching models when "Switch models when a message is flagged" is set to "Ask each time"
  • Changed background subagents to move a shell command to the background after 3 minutes on all providers, so the prompt cache doesn't expire while it runs
  • Changed subagent progress summaries on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, or with telemetry off: on a cold prompt cache, one can now wait up to 5 minutes for the subagent's pending response
  • Changed what a mod attaches at prompt.submit to stay in the user's turn rather than go out as a system message
  • Changed deniedMcpServers URL entries to also block Anthropic-provided servers whose upstream URL matches, and connectors in cloud sessions and on self-hosted runners, where the session is given the connector's own URL; otherwise deny a connector by name
  • Changed the /permissions rule details, built-in rules and delete confirmation views to use the standard dialog; pressing Ctrl+C twice there now goes back or cancels instead of quitting
  • Changed /claude-api managed-agents-onboard to give a new agent's built-in tools, and a quickstart template's MCP tools, the auto permission policy ("Judge risky actions") by default, matching the Claude Console; say "run without asking" to opt out
  • Removed the 2.1.288 fix that kept the model's earlier thinking when resuming a conversation started on 2.1.286 or earlier; that thinking can now be dropped
  • Gateway: Added a log warning when the Google access token from a federation (external_account) credentials file is about to expire
  • Gateway: Improved the log hints about listen.trusted_proxies: they now say to list only a proxy that adds the connecting address to X-Forwarded-For itself
  • Gateway: Improved the warning when AWS CountTokens fails on Amazon Bedrock: it says Claude Code, not the gateway, counts after the 501, and points at IAM only when AWS denies access
  • Self-hosted runner: Added CLAUDE_RUNNER_SPAWN_REASON to the orchestrator's spawn-runner hook environment: why Anthropic sent the request (e.g. runner_lost, resumed); unset when none was sent
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a startup warning when --release-idle-session-min is the last argument with no value (still ignored) or has a value of only spaces (still read as 0)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the orchestrator's log lines: ok session=… now prints at every log level on stdout (was debug only, stderr) with reason=… after jti=…, and nack session=… ends its fields with reason=… after retryable=…; update scripts that match retryable=true: or retryable=false:
  • Remote Control: Fixed a misleading "spawn error: ENOENT" when a session's working folder is missing; the error now names the folder
  • Remote Control: Improved the title a fork of a terminal fork is created with when the app doesn't set one: "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed a window whose sign-in the organization's settings refuse starting a new Claude Code process in the background every minute
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long word in the chat panel's error banner pushing its close button out of view
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in screen to show what Claude Code printed when its sign-in status check fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a No repository option: a cloud session on an Anthropic-hosted environment can now start without picking a repository
  • [Cloud sessions] Added the usual Chrome names to cloud sessions, so tools other than Playwright can find the built-in Chromium through google-chrome and CHROME_PATH
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a New session button to the card shown when a cloud session's environment was deleted, where the message box is hidden
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed reading GitHub Actions logs in cloud sessions: gh run view --log and gh api log requests now get the log in most environments, not an unreachable redirect
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved most Create PR failure messages in cloud and Remote Control sessions: they now give the reason or a link to GitHub instead of saying Try again
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed connector search results to tell Claude that the search covers only part of the connector directory
  • [Remote Control] Fixed side-by-side checkouts of one repository looking identical in the environment menu's Remote Control rows; each now shows its own folder name
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed keyboard focus and screen reader announcements in Claude Tag admin setup; pressing Escape in the connect form no longer also closes the Add dialog
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review analytics page to retry once after a server or network failure, then show a Try again banner instead of empty cards

Added assume_role on mantle upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
